PASSO 1: pense numa coisa que você NÃO f: STEP 1: think of something you did NOT do in the past, but would have done in other circumstances. In English: "I would have gone", "I would have bought". STEP 2: this is another tense that maps neatly onto English: "would have" + participle = the conditional of «haber» + participle: «habría ido», «habría comprado». STEP 3: the conditional of «haber»: habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían. The stem «habr-» is the same as in the future («habré»), and the «-ía» endings are those of the imperfecto of «comer» and «vivir» («comía, vivía»). Every form has an accent on the «í». STEP 4: the participle is the usual one: hablado, comido, vivido; hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto. With «haber» it never agrees. STEP 5: the key use: an action that didn't happen, usually followed by the reason with «pero»: «Habría ido a la fiesta, pero tenía que trabajar» (I would have gone to the party, but I had to work). STEP 6: the same for what you "would have liked": «Me habría gustado viajar más» (I would have liked to travel more). Note: English often says "would have liked TO HAVE travelled"; Spanish keeps the simple infinitive: «me habría gustado viajar». STEP 7: negation and pronouns go before the auxiliary: «No lo habría hecho» (I wouldn't have done it), «Lo habría comprado». STEP 8: one letter changes everything: «había ido» (had gone: you did go, before something else) and «habría ido» (would have gone: you didn't). Listen carefully for «bía» versus «bría».

PASSO 1: o condicional compuesto serve p: STEP 1: the condicional compuesto gives your opinion on something that already happened: «Yo en tu lugar habría dicho la verdad» (If I were you, I would have told the truth). STEP 2: «en tu lugar» (or «en su lugar») — literally "in your place", English "if I were you" — sets up the imaginary situation by itself. STEP 3: many hypotheses don't need the word «si». An expression that implies the condition is enough: «Sin tu ayuda no lo habría conseguido» (Without your help I wouldn't have managed it). STEP 4: the same happens with «con» + noun: «Con más tiempo habría viajado más» (With more time I would have travelled more). STEP 5: also with «de otra manera» (otherwise): «De otra manera, lo habríamos hecho mejor». STEP 6: compare three tenses that look alike: the simple conditional is a hypothesis about the present or future («Iría contigo», I would go with you); the condicional compuesto is a hypothesis about the past («Habría ido contigo», I would have gone with you); the pluscuamperfecto is what really happened before («Había ido contigo», I had gone with you). STEP 7: when someone reports what was going to be finished in the future of a past moment, Spanish uses this tense too: «Dijo que habría terminado para el lunes» (He said he would have finished by Monday). For now, just recognise it. STEP 8: sentences with «si» ("If I had known…" = «Si hubiera sabido…») come in lesson 47 — and there you'll see why "if I would have known" never works in Spanish.

PASSO 1: em português dizemos «deveria t: STEP 1: English says "I should have done", "you could have gone". Spanish keeps the modal and adds the perfect infinitive: «haber» + participle. STEP 2: «debería haber hecho» (should have done), «podría haber ido» (could have gone), «tendría que haber llamado» (I ought to have called). STEP 3: the first verb goes in the simple conditional (debería, podría, tendría) — that's the English "should / could / would". The second is always «haber + participle», which doesn't change — that's the English "have done". STEP 4: a pronoun attaches to the end of «haber»: «debería haberlo dicho» (I should have said it), «podrías haberme llamado» (you could have called me). English puts "it" and "me" at the end; Spanish glues them to «haber». STEP 5: «me habría gustado» + infinitive expresses a wish that didn't come true: «Me habría gustado estudiar música» (I would have liked to study music). STEP 6: you can also say «me gustaría haber» + participle, with the same meaning: «Me gustaría haber estudiado música» (I'd like to have studied music). STEP 7: «habríamos podido» (we could have) talks about a lost possibility: «Habríamos podido llegar antes». STEP 8: «debería haber» is criticism or advice about the past, and softer than the order «tenías que» (you had to).
